author: Mesocricetus Incognitus
text:
You seem like a level headed, resonance and possibility even well-intentioned. 

Don’t believe anyone who calls you a hopeless case. There is hope for you, wherever you live.

Here’s my recommendation. I have no expertise in medicine or psychiatry, neurology, fluid dynamics or geology, so you can’t sue if it fails. 

Take three small rabbit-turds, average dose, and easy to swallow. They’re a little smaller and an aspirin, but round.

Take three every day with at least four ounces of water, vodka, coffee or any drink you prefer. Continue this daily for fourteen days (2 weeks). When your IQ reaches 25 or higher, lower the dosage to two “pills” per day. Keep that up without fail until the end of the year by which time your IQ should have significantly improved. If you test at 50 or above, reduce you medicine to a single pill per day. Discontinue when (and if) you reach the 85+ score.

That is considered “high.functionally retarded.” You no longer require full time supervision.

Good luck. I hope this helps. Unless you live on the north or south pole, you are within a half mile radius of a rabbit. If you are unable to find rabbit “poop pills” you can substitute sheep pellets.

author: IMG Helping Hands
text:
Jordanian Medical Students Who Want US Residency!

Read this detailed guide 👇🏻

What Actually Helps You And What Quietly Hurts You!

Jordan has a strong history of sending successful IMGs to US residency programs. However, increasing competition means that previous success stories do not guarantee future results. Strategic planning is now more important than ever.

🔹 The High Expectation Trap 
Many students from Jordan's leading medical schools see seniors matching successfully and assume the pathway is straightforward. In reality, residency selection has become significantly more competitive. School reputation alone is not enough. Strong USMLE scores, meaningful research, and quality US letters remain essential.
🔹 Starting Too Late 
A common mistake is waiting until after internship to begin serious USMLE preparation. This often creates graduation gaps, delays US clinical experience, and limits research productivity. The strongest applicants begin building their residency profile during medical school rather than after graduation.
🔹 Research Visibility Matters 
Having a single case report or local publication is rarely enough. Residency programs value research that is visible internationally. Students should seek opportunities that can lead to PubMed-indexed publications, systematic reviews, retrospective studies, or quality improvement projects.
🔹 English Fluency vs Interview
 Performance Jordanian students often have excellent English skills. However, interviews reward structured communication rather than fluency alone. Successful applicants answer clearly, directly, and confidently while demonstrating ownership of their accomplishments.
🔹 US Clinical Experience (USCE) 
USCE remains one of the most valuable components of an IMG application. Early planning allows students to secure stronger rotations, stronger mentorship, and stronger Letters of Recommendation. Last-minute rotations often produce weaker outcomes.
🔹 Program Selection Strategy 
Applying broadly without research wastes time and money. Focus on IMG-friendly programs, institutions with a history of training international graduates, and specialties that align with your profile and credentials.
🔹 Specialty Planning 
Internal Medicine, Family Medicine, Pediatrics, Psychiatry, and Neurology remain realistic pathways for many applicants. Highly competitive specialties often require exceptional scores, strong US-based research, and influential professional networks.
🔹 Leverage Jordan's Strengths 
Jordanian medical training frequently provides strong clinical reasoning, tertiary-care hospital exposure, English proficiency, and experience managing diverse patient populations. These strengths become powerful when supported by USMLE performance, research productivity, and US clinical experience.

author: Ahmed Negida, MD PhD 🇪🇬🇺🇲
text: A new study in Annals of Neurology shows that plasma P-tau217 detects Alzheimer co-pathology in Lewy body disorders and predicts cognitive decline in Parkinson's disease. Using a University of Pennsylvania longitudinal cohort — 46 PD and 10 DLB autopsy cases plus 173 clinical PD and 64 controls — investigators found P-tau217 higher in cases with AD co-pathology (median 0.3 vs 0.1, p<0.01) and discriminated co-pathology with an AUC of 0.84. Higher baseline P-tau217 was associated with faster dementia-rating decline and a 1.6-fold risk of cognitive progression (HR 1.597, p=0.003). The findings position plasma P-tau217 as a candidate stratifier for Lewy body disorder trials. doi.org/10.1002/ana.78201

author: Culture War Notes
text:
Vitamin D isn't really a vitamin. It's a steroid hormone that crosses the blood-brain barrier and acts on receptors throughout the brain, including the hippocampus and entorhinal cortex, where Alzheimer's tau accumulates first.
A Framingham Heart Study analysis tracked this for 16 years.
793 adults. Mean baseline age 39. Vitamin D measured 2002-2005. Brain PET imaging 2016-2019.
Higher midlife 25-hydroxyvitamin D was associated with less tau in the brain regions where Alzheimer's pathology starts: entorhinal cortex, parahippocampal gyrus, fusiform gyrus. The relationship was continuous. More D, less tau, smoothly across the range.
The finding is narrow and specific. Vitamin D was associated with tau (the tangle protein) only. There was no association with amyloid (the plaque protein).
The mechanism that fits: vitamin D modulates GSK-3β, the kinase that phosphorylates tau. It's also anti-inflammatory in brain immune cells. These mechanisms are tau-relevant, not particularly amyloid-relevant.
A few qualifications.
This is observational. It cannot prove vitamin D causes lower tau. People developing early pathology may handle vitamin D differently. Reverse causation can't be ruled out.
The clinical cutoff of 30 ng/mL did not reach statistical significance. Only the continuous relationship did. The data doesn't support "below 30 is bad." It supports "more is generally better, smoothly, across the range studied."
The effect size in absolute terms is small. A measurable association, not dramatic protection.
The study did not test supplementation. It measured naturally varying serum levels. Whether pushing your D up with a pill produces the same association is untested.
Practical framing.
Most vitamin D research focused on adults over 65. By 65, tau accumulation has been happening for two decades. The Framingham data suggests the actionable window is earlier.
A reasonable read: test 25-hydroxyvitamin D in your 30s and 40s. The standard reference range labels 30 ng/mL as "sufficient," but in this analysis the association continued above that level. Higher D tracked with less tau across the range.
Reasonable. Not proven causal.
The popular framing of this study is "vitamin D prevents Alzheimer's." The actual finding: a midlife blood marker tracks with a specific brain protein decades later, and the mechanism that fits is narrow and tau-specific.
Mulligan et al., Neurology Open Access, 2026
DOI: 10.1212/WN9.0000000000000057
